steps.label: Principle (when)
steps.body:
Phrases like "as so-and-so said" or "as the saying goes" signal that the story just told illustrates the quote that follows.

The rule:
apparent counterexample just given → "as the saying goes" (or similar) is used inappropriately

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Every choice tells a short story and then tacks on a saying with one of these phrases. So the work is the same five times: read the story, then ask whether what just happened supports the saying or seems to run against it.

If the story supports the saying, the phrase is doing its job. If the story looks like an exception to the saying, the phrase is misused, and that is the answer the stem wants. Don't get pulled into whether the saying is wise. We only care whether this story fits it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find the story whose events point the opposite way from its saying: things go one way, and the quote that follows claims something the story just contradicted.

notes.body: Fatima knows enough mathematics to see how much will stay unsolved. That's the saying in action: you need to know a lot before you see how little you know. The story illustrates it, so the phrase is used properly.

Harold has done the same thing many times before. That's selfishness as predictable as gravity, so the quote matches the story. The friends' surprise doesn't change that Harold's behavior was calculable.

Roger won't buy the expensive vacuum because Roger is frugal and would never forgive the spending. "A penny saved is a penny earned" is the frugal person's motto, so the story illustrates it and the phrase is used properly.

Sharon loves cats, and Sharon's husband, despite the allergy, still sometimes comes along to cat shows. Sharing a life with Sharon means sharing what Sharon loves, at least a little. The story illustrates the saying.

Raoul's trip ended with a broken leg and two weeks in the hospital. That didn't end well, so "All's well that ends well" has no illustration here. The story is an apparent counterexample, and putting "as the saying goes" after it is the misuse the principle describes.

why: Principle step was garbled shorthand and Evaluate carried an em dash; notes were already sound and are kept (C lightly extended).

steps.label: Situation and Analysis
steps.body:
Situation: someone in a cold climate buys a coat that is stylish but not warm, to look sophisticated.

Analysis: people are sometimes willing to sacrifice sensual comfort or pleasure for the sake of appearances.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Line the analysis up against the coat. The coat buyer gives up warmth, which is comfort. The coat buyer does it to look sophisticated, which is appearances.

So the analysis has two ingredients, and a matching situation needs both:
1. A real sacrifice: the person picks something that feels, tastes, or works worse for them.
2. A reason about how they look to others.

A choice with only one ingredient doesn't fit. Someone who sacrifices comfort for the planet fails the second. Someone who wants to impress but gives up nothing fails the first.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a person who knowingly takes the less pleasant option so that other people will be impressed.

notes.body: The person chooses a car over quick, reliable public transportation, but nothing says they give up comfort or pleasure, and nothing says they do it to look good to anyone. The analysis needs both pieces: a sacrifice, made for the sake of appearances.
The parent picks the car seat because it is more colorful and more comfortable for the child. That gains comfort instead of sacrificing it, and the choice isn't made to impress anyone.

Check both ingredients. The sacrifice: the couple passes over their favorite wine, which tastes better, so they give up pleasure. The reason: they think the other wine "will impress their dinner guests," which is appearances. That is the coat again: a worse experience in exchange for a better image. The "less expensive" detail is extra; the taste is the pleasure being given up.
Keeping the thermostat low does sacrifice comfort, but the reason is concern about environmental damage, not appearances. The analysis requires the sacrifice to be made for how one looks to others.

The acrobat does care about appearances, since the outfit is meant to impress the audience. But the acrobat gives up nothing: the circus pays, and nothing suggests the outfit is less comfortable or pleasant. With no sacrifice of comfort or pleasure, the analysis doesn't fit.

why: Single step restated the analysis with no evaluation or prediction, and the correct-answer note never named the sacrifice.

steps.label: Given
steps.body: In a recent study, a group of young children were taught the word “stairs” while walking up and down a flight of stairs. Later that day, when the children were shown a video of a person climbing a ladder, they all called the ladder stairs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Describe what happened in general terms, since the right principle won't mention stairs or ladders.

How did the children learn the word? By walking up and down the stairs, so they learned it through how the object is used.

What did they do later? They called a ladder "stairs." A ladder is a different object, but it is used the same way: you climb it.

So the study shows children stretching a word from the object they learned it on to a different object with the same use. Notice what the study does not show. It doesn't compare teaching methods, so it can't tell us how children learn "best." And it has one group at one age, so it can't tell us anything about age.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Something like: children who learn a word through how an object is used sometimes apply the word to a different object that is used in a similar way.

notes.body: The children learned the word while walking up and down real stairs. A describes children who hear a word without seeing the object, which is not what happened in the study.
The study shows children misapplying a word, not how they learn words best. Nothing in it compares ways of teaching, so it can't illustrate a claim about how children "best" learn words.

C is about how early in life a child meets an object and how easily the child learns not to misuse the word. The study has one group of young children and never compares ages. It also shows the children misusing the word, not learning to avoid misuse, so neither half of C has an example here.

Match D to the study piece by piece. "learn a word by observing how the object denoted by that word is used": the children learned "stairs" while walking up and down stairs. "sometimes apply that word to a different object": they called a ladder stairs. "that is similarly used": both are things you climb. Every part of D has a matching fact, and D stays modest with "sometimes," which is all one study can illustrate.
The study doesn't compare learning conditions, so it can't show when children "best" learn names. It also never says whether other objects were present when the children learned "stairs."

why: Only a restated stimulus with no principle or prediction; C and D notes were one-line verdicts.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Democratic societies in which there is widespread discontent more often blame their politicians than they do other powerful figures who are at least as responsible for those societies’ woes.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: This [blaming of politicians] is not primarily because politicians are more familiar to people than are other powerful figures. People blame politicians because they feel that they have more power over politicians than they have over other powerful figures.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a case, and the stem wants the general rule it illustrates. So strip out the specifics and keep the moving parts.

Who gets blamed more? Politicians, which in general terms are publicly known people.
Why? Not mainly because they are familiar. The author sets that explanation aside. The reason is that people feel they have more power over politicians.

So the case links two things: feeling power over someone and blaming that someone more. The author also hands us a trap in advance. Familiarity is named only to be rejected, so an answer that makes familiarity the driver of blame is fighting the stimulus.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: We're looking for a generalization like: people are more likely to blame a public figure when they feel they have power over that figure.

notes.body: A contrasts who really has the most power with who the public thinks has the most power. The case is about power people feel they have over a figure, not how powerful a figure seems to be. It never says the public misjudges who is most powerful, so A's contrast has no example here.

B ties familiarity to how much power people ascribe to someone. The stimulus sets familiarity aside as not the main reason for blame, and never says familiarity changes how powerful anyone seems. B also leaves out blame, which is the behavior the whole case describes.

C is the tempting one, because politicians are well known and they do get blamed. But C makes being well known the reason for blame, and the stimulus says the blame is "not primarily because politicians are more familiar." The case illustrates a different cause, felt power. An answer that adopts the explanation the author rejects can't be what the case illustrates.

D is about whether public figures are blamed enough for the problems they cause. The stimulus never judges whether the blame is the right amount; it explains why one group gets more blame than another. If anything, politicians get more blame than figures who are at least as responsible, which points away from "not held sufficiently responsible."

Match the parts. "a publicly known person" covers politicians. "someone over whom they feel they have power" is the author's own reason. "more inclined to blame" is the behavior in the case. E turns the case into a rule by swapping the specific group for a general category while keeping the cause the author endorses. Test it by plugging the case back in: people feel power over politicians, so they blame politicians more. That is the stimulus.

why: Evaluate called the two explanations equally plausible and used em dashes, Goal mislabelled the answer an assumption, and notes were padded explicit-Standard register.

steps.label: Situation
steps.body: Future overall demand for professors can be predicted with reasonable accuracy from current birth rates.

steps.label: However...
steps.body: The accuracy of predictions of future demand for music professors is lower, and that for jazz studies professors lower still.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: In this situation we're comparing a prediction about a general group, professors, to a prediction about a subset of that group, music professors. We then compare the prediction about music professors to a prediction about a subset of music professors, namely jazz studies professors. The demand for the overall group can be predicted reasonably well by birth rates. But as we look at each smaller, more specific subset, there's a decrease in the ability to accurately predict demand.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: We're expecting an answer to state that we have a greater ability to predict something about a general group, with less and less ability to make accurate predictions as we look at specific categories within groups.

notes.body: A ties precision to how detailed and complete the evidence is. The stimulus never describes the evidence behind the music or jazz predictions, let alone says it is more or less detailed. The only thing we see change is the target, from professors to music professors to jazz studies professors. A case where the evidence never varies can't illustrate a rule about evidence.

Line up the three predictions. All professors: reasonably accurate. Music professors, a narrower group: less accurate. Jazz studies professors, narrower still: less accurate again. Each step down makes the prediction more specific and less accurate, which is B read in reverse: the more general the level, the more accurate. On illustrate questions, name what changes across the case and what changes with it, then find the answer that links those two things.

The situation does not involve temporal distance. All predictions are about the future from the same present point. Accuracy varies because of specificity, not because some events are further in the future.

D has A's problem with a different outcome word: confidence instead of precision. Nothing in the stimulus says the evidence for one prediction is more detailed or complete than the evidence for another, so the case shows no example of better evidence earning more confidence. What changes is how specific the prediction is.

The situation shows the opposite: predictions based on general trends (birth rates) are reasonably accurate for overall professor demand. This answer claims such predictions are "unlikely to be accurate," which directly contradicts the first sentence of the stimulus.

why: A and D notes claimed all three predictions use birth rates, which the stimulus never says, and carried em dashes; B note did not teach the matching move.

steps.label: The gain
steps.body: Increased productivity resulting from greater efficiency [from Taylor's methods] has led to increases in most workers' standards of living.

steps.label: The change
steps.body: At the same time, Taylor's methods have tended to make these workers' jobs routine and repetitive.

steps.label: The loss
steps.body: That change has robbed their work of some of the intrinsic worth it possessed when it emphasized creativity and talent.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This isn't an argument. Nothing here is offered as proof of anything else. It is a description of a tradeoff, and the stem asks for the generalization it fits.

Taylor's methods did two things at once. They raised efficiency and productivity, and that raised most workers' standards of living: a material gain. They also made jobs routine and repetitive, which took away some of the work's intrinsic worth: a loss in what the work itself is like.

So a matching generalization needs both sides: one development, a gain for workers in one respect, a loss for workers in another. Also watch the strength. The stimulus says "most" workers and "some of" the intrinsic worth, and it never says the gain causes the loss. An answer that claims more than that won't fit cleanly.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Something like: a change in industry can help workers in one way, such as their standard of living, while making their work worse in another way, such as how satisfying it is.

notes.body: "It" refers back to efficiency, so A says some measures that seem to boost efficiency actually hurt efficiency. The stimulus says the opposite about Taylorism: it produced "greater efficiency" and increased productivity. The loss in the case is to the work's intrinsic worth, not to efficiency.

Match each piece. "Some developments in industry" is Taylorism. "benefit workers financially" is the rise in standards of living from increased productivity. "less rewarding in other respects" is the loss of intrinsic worth when the jobs became routine and repetitive. B keeps both sides of the tradeoff and stays modest with "Some" and "can," which is exactly what one case can illustrate.

C swaps in a different loss: workers devoting less effort to their jobs. The stimulus says the jobs became routine and repetitive, not that workers try less, and a repetitive job can take plenty of effort. The loss in the case is the work's intrinsic worth, which C never mentions.

D is the closest trap because it uses both sides of the stimulus: higher living standards and something like valuing the job less. But D says a rise in living standards "will likely involve" a drop in how much workers value their jobs, as if the first brings the second. In the case, both came from Taylor's methods; the higher living standard didn't produce the routine work. D also stretches "some of the intrinsic worth" into how much workers value their jobs "overall," and the stimulus never says what workers themselves value.

E compares two kinds of workers, highly creative ones and average ones, and says the creative ones are sometimes less efficient. The stimulus compares the same jobs before and after Taylorism, not different workers. It never measures anyone's creativity or says creative workers are slower.

why: Breakdown forced a description into argument roles with a garbled conclusion and an Evaluate that critiqued an assumption; notes were padded with em dashes.

steps.label: Conclusion (thus)
steps.body: The discovery of powerful cures for certain high-incidence forms of cancer would probably trigger an increase in behaviors such as smoking and overexposure to sun that are known to increase the risks of such cancers.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Drivers of SUVs correctly believe that they are at less risk of serious injury in an accident, and such drivers therefore tend to drive less carefully than they would in more traditional vehicles.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author is arguing by analogy. If we want, we can lay out the parts to help us articulate any missing ingredients.
```
SUVs                     Cures for Cancer
drivers know their       (people know their
risk of serious injury   risk of dying from
in an accident is low    such cancer is low)
so, the drivers drive    people would smoke
less carefully than      more and not use
they otherwise would     sunscreen, despite
                         the higher cancer risk
```
Since the argument is by analogy and the question stem is asking for an underlying principle, we should probably try to articulate the underlying general idea that operates in both halves of the analogy.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Let's look for something like, "If you know you're better protected from the potential downside of risky behavior X, then you're more likely to do X."

notes.body: A is about people who see several ways to reduce a risk and take only the one they think works best. The journalist never mentions people choosing between safety measures. The argument is about protection leading people to take more risks, so both A's trigger (several measures available) and its outcome (picking just one) miss.

Set B beside both halves of the analogy. "ways to protect people from the consequences" is the SUV's lower injury risk and the cancer cure. "behaviors that would normally harm them" is careless driving, smoking, and too much sun. "less careful to avoid such behaviors" is drivers driving less carefully and people smoking and tanning more. B is the Goal in general terms: protection from the downside makes the risky behavior more likely. When the reasoning is an analogy, the right principle is the one rule that covers both halves.

C says people take special care with behaviors they think will likely seriously injure them, and none with behaviors they think are harmless. The journalist's people don't think careless driving or smoking is harmless; they think the risk is lower or the disease curable. C also never says that reducing a risk makes people less careful, which is the journalist's whole move.

D compares activities with known risks to activities of unknown risk. In the journalist's examples the risks are known: SUV drivers "correctly" believe the risk is lower, and smoking and sun exposure are "known to increase the risks" of cancer. What changes is how bad the consequences are, not whether the risk is known, so D's comparison never appears.

E tempts if you reason a step ahead: a cure makes cancer a lesser harm, so other desires win out. But the journalist never sorts harms into serious and lesser and never mentions competing desires. The reasoning runs from more protection to less care. E mentions neither protection nor a change in behavior, so it doesn't capture the link both of the journalist's examples rely on.

why: Breakdown sound and kept; notes were padded explicit-Standard register with em dashes, and the A and C notes misquoted the choices.

steps.label: Principle
steps.body:
```
Action would increase likelihood
of physical harm to others         govt. justified
and                             →  in interfering
Not motivated by desire            with person's
to help others                     action
```

steps.label: Evaluate / Goal
steps.body:
A rule can only prove its right side. Here that is one outcome: the government is justified in interfering. So any answer that concludes the government is not justified is out before we check anything else. Showing that the triggers are missing doesn't prove the opposite outcome; it just means the rule doesn't apply.

For an answer that concludes interference is justified, check that the facts in the choice establish both triggers:
1. The action would increase the likelihood of physical harm to others.
2. The action is not motivated by a desire to help others.

Watch the qualifiers. "Physical" rules out harm to looks or money. "Others" rules out harm to the person acting.

Goal: a judgment where someone acting for their own reasons does something likely to physically hurt other people, and the conclusion is that the government is justified in stepping in.

notes.body: A concludes the government is unjustified in interfering with Jerry's moviemaking. Our principle can only prove that interference is justified. Jerry's facts (no harm, a motive to benefit the children) show the triggers are missing, but a missing trigger never proves the opposite outcome. The principle simply has nothing to say about Jerry.

B has the right kind of outcome, a city council justified in acting, but the harm is aesthetic: a property is "less pleasing" to look at. The principle needs an increased likelihood of physical harm to others. B also never establishes the neighbor's motive; forgetting to mow isn't shown to be anything at all.

C is tempting because it involves physical injury and a government rule. But ask who gets hurt when a rider skips the helmet: the rider. The principle requires harm to others, so the first trigger fails. C also says nothing about the rider's motive, so the second trigger is never established either.

D gets the second trigger: Zabziew's research is motivated by profit, "not by the desire to benefit customers." The first trigger fails. Being "of little help to people suffering from serious illness" is not increasing the likelihood of physical harm to them. Failing to help someone isn't harming them, so the principle never fires.

Check both triggers against the facts. Physical harm to others: the speech "would most likely have caused a riot and people would have gotten hurt." Not motivated by a desire to help others: Jill's aim was to further Jill's own political ambitions. Both are established, so the rule delivers its outcome, and E's conclusion matches it: the government was justified in preventing the speech. That is the move for every conform question with a conditional rule: confirm each trigger with facts in the choice, then make sure the conclusion is the rule's right side.

why: E note described a pesticide speech that is not in the choice, D note misquoted Zabziew, Evaluate wrongly implied a non-government actor could be dismissed, and notes carried em dashes.
